After the 1970s, Philippine National Program sought to protect the Ifugawa rice terraces,
recognized as both cultural heritage and productive farmland, while increasing food output for
a growing population.
Officials reason that direct payments would keep farmers on the terraces, and that modern
concrete canals would deliver water more reliably than the traditional network of small,
adjustable ditches. At the time, both goals appeared compatible. Heritage preservation through
income support and agricultural modernization through better infrastructure seemed like a single
coherent approach. The programs reflected a broader policy view that combining cash incentives
with physical improvements, could stabilize rural landscapes and raise productivity
without displacing local communities. Decision makers worked from the information available,
visible terrorist deterioration and periodic water shortages, and treated the two interventions
as mutually reinforcing. They saw the stipends as a way to retain labor that might otherwise leave
for urban work. They saw the concrete as a durable fix that would reduce the hours spent rebuilding
building earth and banks after each monsoon.
Programs rolled out across EFUGAO municipalities, offering maintenance stipends tied to terrace
upkeep and grants or loans for constructing concrete irrigation channels.
Early reports noted higher rice yields in areas where the new canals reached fields consistently.
Proponents highlighted the dual benefit of preserved cultural landscapes and improved harvests.
Some local observers noted that the concrete structures altered the gradual, distributed
flow patterns long-managed by hand.
Construction crews poured the channels along existing alignments first, then extended them
to steeper parcels that had previously relied on bamboo split pipe diversions.
Once the forms were set, the fixed gradient and smooth interior walls produced higher flow
velocities than the rough, porous surfaces of the older ditches.
Farmers accepted the stipends because they offset the cost of weeding and replanting that
had become harder as household sizes shrank.
The rigid concrete canals concentrated water into fewer, faster moving paths, rather
than spreading it across the stepped pond system as the older channels had done.
Run off therefore carried more soil into the ponds, accelerating siltation, and reducing
the terrace's ability to hold water through the growing season.
As viability declined, many households shifted labor toward cash crop vegetables planted

The current landscape shows a patchwork.
Some lower terraces remain productive under mixed systems, while upper sections have
